query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating approximately 10 wt% MoS2 into a high-entropy alloy matrix via powder metallurgical methods will reduce both friction and wear by forming a robust solid-lubricating film across a broad temperature range (up to at least ~800 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi) consolidated without solid-lubricant additives.
generation.intervention: Add MoS2 (~10 wt%) to the alloy powder during feedstock preparation (e.g., mechanical alloying or spark plasma sintering) to uniformly distribute the solid-lubricant phase.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding contact in ambient or inert atmosphere, from room temperature to ~800 °C, under moderate loads and sliding speeds (e.g., 5–10 N, 0.1–0.5 m/s).
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a lubricious MoS2-based tribofilm at the surface, maintained by shear during contact.
generation.mechanism: Shear-induced slipping of stacked MoS2 lamellae creates a low-friction interface, reducing adhesive and abrasive wear. Oxide formation is suppressed or minimized, retaining effective lubrication over a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coefficient of friction decreases by roughly 30–50% and wear rate can be lowered by an order of magnitude versus the undoped HEA, observed consistently up to ~800 °C.
generation.baseline: An equivalent HEA processed under the same conditions but without MoS2 doping, evaluated using identical tribological tests.
generation.boundary: Benefits may diminish at temperatures above ~800 °C where MoS2 decomposition accelerates, or under exceedingly high loads and speeds that exceed the stable limits of the tribofilm.
generation.uncertainty: Limited direct testing data exist above 400 °C in some studies; more high-temperature tribological evaluations are needed to confirm the persistence of the MoS2-based film and its lubricating effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AlCoCrFeNiTi-based samples via spark plasma sintering: a control set without MoS2 and an experimental set containing 10 wt% MoS2. Subject both sets to pin-on-disk tribological testing from 25 °C to 800 °C in increments (e.g., 200 °C intervals).
measurements: Coefficient of friction over test duration at each temperature
Wear volumes/track depths measured via post-test profilometry or microscopy
Surface chemical composition analysis of worn surfaces via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MoS2-doped samples do not exhibit measurably reduced friction or wear when compared to the undoped alloy, or if no lubricating tribofilm is observed under SEM/EDS across the tested temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature. A further improvement of wear behaviour can be achieved by lubrication. Solid lubricants can be applied to reduce the coefficient of friction (COF). Powder metallurgical technologies enable the incorporation of solid lubricants by processing powder blends. The suitability of different powder production routes for the production of homogeneous and spherical HEA feedstock has been investigated, whereas inert gas atomisation showed the best results []. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) technology is appropriate for the fast production of dense material. In comparison to other sintering techniques, the current activated process enables high heating rates and a low sintering temperature. The processed material exhibits a low porosity and the absence of grain coarsening [,]. The suitability of the SPS processing route for HEAs has already been mentioned [,], whereas the approach of incorporating solid lubricants has only been investigated for a few HEA systems [,]. Beside graphite, MoS2 is one of the most commonly used solid lubricants, showing good lubricating performance below 400 °C [,,]. chosen.why: Introducing MoS2 provides a well-known, robust solid-lubricant mechanism to lower friction and wear by forming lubricious films that remain effective at various temperatures. Powder-metallurgy-based doping is a straightforward, industry-accepted approach that precisely addresses the question’s goal of consistently reducing friction and wear across a wide temperature range for self-lubricating high-entropy-alloy components.
